CausalChain: Chronic viral infection/oxidative stress -> Upregulation of m6A methyltransferases -> Increased m6A modification on specific lncRNAs -> Altered lncRNA secondary structure -> Enhanced binding of lncRNAs to epigenetic modifiers (e.g., EZH2) -> Epigenetic silencing of tumor suppressor genes -> Promotion of HCC proliferation and metastasis
Hypothesis: m6A modifications function as a regulatory switch that converts tumor-suppressive lncRNAs into oncogenic mediators in HCC by altering their binding interactions with epigenetic regulators, thereby silencing tumor suppressor genes and driving cancer progression.
Abstract: In this study, we propose that dynamic N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modifications on long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) serve as a molecular switch that determines their functional output in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Under chronic hepatic stress conditions, such as persistent viral infection and oxidative injury, m6A methyltransferases are upregulated, leading to enhanced m6A deposition on specific lncRNAs. This modification alters the secondary structure of these lncRNAs and modulates their interaction with key epigenetic regulators, notably EZH2. As a consequence, the m6A-modified lncRNAs preferentially recruit EZH2 to tumor suppressor gene loci, promoting their epigenetic silencing and thereby accelerating malignant phenotypes—such as uncontrolled proliferation and metastasis—in HCC. Targeting this m6A-lncRNA-epigenetic axis could provide a novel therapeutic opportunity for HCC management.
